question: Tell me about a time you had to resolve a significant conflict between stakeholders while driving a critical project forward.
answer: At Meta in Q2 2024, I was the TPM leading the Payments Infrastructure Migration affecting 500M users globally. Three months into the 9-month project, a critical conflict emerged between our VP of Engineering (Sarah Chen) and VP of Product (David Kim) that threatened to derail our $8M initiative. Engineering wanted to pause all feature development for 4 months to focus purely on infrastructure stability, citing 3 production incidents in the prior week. Product refused, arguing that our committed roadmap to launch Buy Now Pay Later by Q4 was non-negotiable for revenue targets—pausing would cost us $15M in projected Q4 revenue. Both executives escalated to our CTO demanding I 'pick a side.' The conflict was intensifying daily, with their teams now in open warfare—engineers refusing to attend product planning meetings, product managers bypassing engineering in decisions. I had 72 hours before our board meeting where the CTO would be asked about project status. My task was to resolve this VP-level conflict, preserve both the infrastructure migration timeline and the product roadmap, maintain team morale across 45 people, and present a unified plan to the board. Here's what I did. First, I didn't pick a side—I reframed the problem. I scheduled separate 1:1s with Sarah and David, not to mediate, but to deeply understand their actual fears. With Sarah, I discovered the real issue wasn't the migration—it was that her team felt product was treating infrastructure as an afterthought, and the recent incidents had damaged their credibility with the CTO. With David, I learned he was under extreme pressure from the CEO to hit Q4 numbers, and any delay would result in missing his annual bonus tied to revenue targets. The conflict wasn't technical—it was trust and incentives. I proposed a solution neither had considered: a hybrid dual-track approach. I created a detailed plan where we'd split the engineering team—60% on infrastructure (Sarah's priority), 40% on BNPL features (David's priority)—but with a critical twist. I proposed that Sarah's team own the BNPL launch infrastructure, making them directly accountable for product success. This gave Engineering skin in the game for revenue, and Product a forcing function to care about infrastructure stability. I presented this to both VPs together in a 2-hour working session. Initially, both resisted—Sarah said 60/40 wasn't enough, David said he needed 80% on features. I held firm and brought data: I showed that with the dual-track approach plus 2 contractor engineers I'd get approved, we could deliver both. I also proposed a shared success metric they'd both be measured on: 'Zero revenue-impacting incidents during BNPL launch.' This aligned their incentives. After intense negotiation, both agreed. I didn't stop there. I established a weekly 'Product-Infra Council' meeting with both VPs, myself as facilitator, and clear decision-making protocols to prevent future escalations. I created a public dashboard tracking both infrastructure health AND feature progress, ensuring transparency. I also ran a team offsite bringing both orgs together to rebuild trust through collaborative planning. We delivered the infrastructure migration on time in November 2024 with zero production incidents during the final 4 months. BNPL launched on schedule in October, generating $12M in Q4 revenue (beating the $15M projection wasn't realistic, but we minimized loss). Team engagement scores increased from 6.2 to 8.1 during this period. The Product-Infra Council framework I established was adopted by 8 other product teams at Meta. Both Sarah and David publicly credited me in their year-end reviews, and I was promoted to Senior TPM in December 2024. What I learned: VP-level conflicts are rarely about the stated problem—they're about fear, incentives, and trust. My job as TPM isn't to pick sides, but to reframe the problem in a way where both sides can win. The dual-track approach with shared accountability became my go-to pattern for resolving stakeholder conflicts.

question: Tell me about a time you had to debug a complex production issue under time pressure and explain your systematic approach to root cause analysis.
answer: At Stripe in March 2024, I was the TPM for Payment Processing Infrastructure serving 50M transactions daily worth $2B in total payment volume. At 2:47 AM on a Saturday, I got paged—our fraud detection system was rejecting 23% of legitimate transactions (normal rate: 0.8%), costing merchants approximately $180K per hour in lost revenue. Our SLA guaranteed 99.95% uptime, and we were violating it. The on-call engineer had been debugging for 90 minutes with no progress and escalated to me. I had 4 hours before our VP of Engineering would be paged, and every minute meant $3K in merchant losses. The system involved 12 microservices, 4 databases, 3 ML models, and traffic across 6 AWS regions. My task was to identify the root cause, implement a fix, and prevent recurrence—all while keeping merchants and our executive team informed. Here's my systematic approach. I didn't start with code—I started with data. I opened our Datadog dashboard and pulled transaction error rates segmented by region, merchant size, payment method, and timestamp. Within 15 minutes, I identified a pattern: 94% of false rejections were Visa transactions in the US-East region, and they started exactly at 1:23 AM UTC. This ruled out a gradual degradation (like a memory leak) and pointed to a discrete event. I hypothesized three possibilities: (1) Visa API change, (2) our fraud ML model deployment, (3) database replication lag in US-East. I validated each hypothesis systematically. I checked our deployment logs—no fraud model changes at 1:23 AM. I checked Datadog APM traces for Visa API latency—normal response times. I checked our PostgreSQL replication lag dashboard—bingo. US-East read replica was 47 seconds behind master (normal: <2 seconds). This meant fraud checks were reading stale data, causing legitimate transactions to be flagged because user risk scores hadn't updated yet. But why did replication lag spike at 1:23 AM? I SSH'd into the database instance and ran 'pg_stat_replication' to check replication slots. I found the issue: a long-running analytics query from our data science team had started at 1:20 AM and was holding a replication slot, blocking updates. The query was scanning 8B rows to generate a weekly fraud report. I had two options: (1) kill the query and fix immediately, (2) investigate further. I chose option 1 for speed—I killed the query, replication caught up in 90 seconds, and false rejection rate dropped to 0.9% by 2:52 AM. Total incident duration: 2 hours 5 minutes. Merchant loss: approximately $360K. But I didn't stop there. I needed to prevent recurrence. I dug into why the analytics query was running on the production replica. I found that our data science team had been granted read access to prod replicas 6 months ago for 'quick analysis,' and no query timeout limits were set. This was a ticking time bomb. I immediately implemented three fixes: (1) Added query timeout of 30 seconds on all read replicas, (2) Created a separate analytics replica with lower replication priority so it couldn't block prod traffic, (3) Wrote a runbook for on-call engineers on how to identify replication lag issues, including the exact commands I used. I also scheduled a postmortem meeting for Monday with data science, engineering, and DBA teams. In the postmortem, I led the team through a '5 Whys' analysis, which revealed our monitoring gaps: we had alerts for replication lag >60 seconds, but not for long-running queries. I proposed and implemented a new alert: any query >10 seconds on prod replicas triggers a Slack notification to on-call. I also created a quarterly 'database health review' process where DBAs and TPMs review slow query logs together. Six months later, we had zero replication-related incidents. The runbook I created was adopted across 15 other services at Stripe. I presented this case study at our internal 'Debugging Excellence' workshop, and it became required training for all new TPMs. The VP of Engineering personally thanked me for the systematic approach and preventing what could have been a multi-million dollar outage. What I learned: debugging under pressure requires discipline—resist the urge to randomly try fixes. Start with data, form hypotheses, validate systematically. And always think beyond the immediate fix—ask 'how do we prevent this class of failure forever?' The monitoring gaps I identified saved Stripe an estimated $2M in potential future incidents based on similar patterns in our incident history.
